@graph.name: Junk Removal Operations
@graph.description: Junk removal operations: the removal of unwanted non-hazardous items from homes, estates, rentals, and businesses, run as one coordinated plan — survey, flat-rate quote, scheduling, removal, sorting, routing, and lawful disposal, with a final walkthrough of the cleared space. The survey: items are inventoried where they sit — room, floor, and access noted — in person, or through the free film-only video walkthrough survey room, where the customer films and a person makes the estimate; nothing is auto-priced. The quote: the full scope of each job is reviewed — the items, the distance, the manpower, and the equipment — and priced at one flat rate in writing before work begins, never by the hour. The removal: crews lift, carry, and load from where items sit — basements, attics, garages, upper floors, and yards — protecting floors, walls, and doorways on the path out, and taking standard furniture apart when a piece has to come apart to leave safely. The sorting: after pickup, every load is sorted before anything is thrown out — usable goods are routed toward donation, recyclable materials toward recycling, regulated-stream items toward the facilities that handle them, and only the remainder toward disposal. The routing: donation channels take usable furniture and household goods; recyclers take scrap metal, cardboard, and electronics; appliances that contain refrigerant are routed so the refrigerant is recovered by certified technicians before the appliance is processed, as federal rules require; construction and demolition debris goes to facilities that accept it; what is left goes to a transfer station or landfill. The boundary: hazardous and regulated waste is never loaded — no wet paint or solvents, no fuels or motor oil, no chemicals or pesticides, no pressurized tanks, no asbestos-containing material, no medical or biohazard waste. Heavy pieces are not forced through this service: a gun safe or another high-mass asset of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs moves under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with L/360 floor-deflection analysis, and pianos move under the piano, antique and white-glove service. The quote path: Get My Flat Rate Quote — the Short (Quick Quote) form by default or the Detailed Project form, switching in place with From, To and What's moving preserved — or the free survey room; a person makes every estimate. Founded June 2010; dispatch runs the I-81, I-66 and I-70 corridor network from both branches.

@graph.name: Removal Scope & Load Operations
@graph.description: Removal scope and load operations: the item classes this service clears, and how each class is handled on the job. Furniture: sofas, sectionals, recliners, dressers, wardrobes, dining sets, bed frames, and entertainment centers — carried out whole where the path allows, taken apart when a piece must come apart to leave safely. Mattresses and box springs: bagged or wrapped for the carry out, and routed to facilities that accept them. Appliances: washers, dryers, ranges, dishwashers, refrigerators, freezers, and water heaters — disconnected from their hookups as part of the pickup where the connection is a standard household connection; appliances that contain refrigerant are routed so the refrigerant is recovered by certified technicians before processing, under the federal rule recorded in the compliance node. Electronics and e-waste: televisions, computers, and small electronics, routed to electronics recycling. Exercise equipment: treadmills, ellipticals, weight benches, and racks — taken apart for the carry when needed. Hot tubs and spas: the tub is drained and disconnected from power and water before the appointment; the crew cuts and hauls the shell in sections. Yard debris: brush, branches, fencing, and playsets. Renovation and construction debris: drywall, lumber, plywood, flooring, carpet, cabinets, countertops, and fixtures — dense material such as concrete, brick, and soil is planned by weight, because weight, not space, governs how much a truck can carry in one load. Whole-property material: bagged household junk and accumulated contents from garages, basements, attics, estates, evictions, and office cleanouts. Access is recorded at the survey — stairs, long carries, elevators, and tight doorways are part of the scope the flat rate is written against, never a surprise added on the day.

@graph.name: Junk & Debris Taxonomy
@graph.description: Junk and debris taxonomy: the material classes a removal load is sorted into, each with its destination class. Household furniture and upholstery — donation when usable, disposal when spent. Mattresses and foam — facilities that accept mattresses, including mattress recycling where it operates. Wood and lumber — clean wood recycling or disposal with the load. Metal, ferrous and non-ferrous — scrap recycling, graded and weighed by type. Appliances without refrigerant — metal recycling. Appliances with refrigerant — refrigerant recovery by certified technicians first, then processing. Electronics and e-waste — electronics recycling; cathode-ray-tube screens are a special-handling class inside it. Paper and cardboard — recycling. Textiles and clothing — donation when usable. Yard organics — brush, branches, and green waste routing. Construction and demolition classes — drywall and gypsum, lumber, flooring, carpet, roofing shingles, masonry and concrete, and fixtures — to facilities that accept construction and demolition debris. Mixed household junk — sorted at the load level, with the recyclable and donatable fractions pulled before disposal. Excluded classes, never loaded: hazardous chemicals and solvents, wet paint, fuels and motor oil, pesticides, pressurized containers, asbestos-containing material, lead paint material, and medical or biohazard waste — each belongs to a licensed handler or a household hazardous waste route, named in the compliance node.

@graph.name: Dispatch, Routing & Disposal Chain

Each job is dispatched against one date — the removal date — with the crew, truck, and equipment matched to the surveyed scope. The routing chain after pickup, by facility class and never by an unnamed shortcut: usable furniture, working appliances, tools, and household goods go toward donation channels; scrap metal, cardboard, clean wood, and electronics go toward recycling processors and scrap yards; refrigerant-bearing appliances go toward processing where certified technicians recover the refrigerant first; construction and demolition debris goes toward facilities that accept it; mattresses go toward facilities that accept them; and the sorted remainder goes to a transfer station or landfill. Sorting happens before any compaction, because once a load is crushed together nothing in it can be salvaged. No donation partner, recycler, or disposal account is named in this dataset — the chain is published by facility class, and no partnership is claimed.

@graph.name: Commercial Terms & Cost Drivers
@graph.description: Commercial terms and cost drivers for junk removal. The company's terms: every job is surveyed first; the full scope — the items, the distance, the manpower, and the equipment — is reviewed, and the job is priced at one flat rate in writing before work begins. The flat rate is the price for the job as scoped; the company does not price junk removal by the hour, and no rate card, per-item price list, or truckload price is published — the price of a job is the written flat rate for that job. Quotes come through Get My Flat Rate Quote (Short or Detailed form) or the free video walkthrough survey room, and a person makes every estimate; nothing is auto-priced. Cost drivers, as the industry names them and as the scope review weighs them: the volume the load occupies; the weight and density of the material (disposal facilities bill haulers by weight, so dense debris prices differently from bulky furniture); the labor and access the pickup needs (stairs, long carries, disassembly); the distance to the property and onward to disposal; and the disposal fees the load itself carries. Domain facts, labeled as such — industry pricing models and published figures, never this company's prices: most of the industry prices by truck volume in fractions (minimum pickup, quarter, half, three-quarter, full load) — 2026 U.S. pricing guides publish typical ranges of roughly $70–$175 for a minimum pickup, $150–$300 for a quarter load, $250–$550 for a half load, and $550–$1,000 for a full truckload, in trucks of roughly 15–18 cubic yards (Housecall Pro and MyQuoteIQ 2026 guides); other haulers price by weight per ton, by the item for single pickups, or by the hour at published guide rates of $50–$150 — the hourly model this company does not use, because an hourly price is not known until the job is done and a flat rate is.

@graph.name: Buyer Personas & Trigger Events
@graph.description: Buyer personas and trigger events for junk removal. Homeowners clearing a house for sale or after a move — the trigger is a date: a listing, a closing, a move day. Downsizers and senior transitions, where a household's accumulated decades are sorted into keep, donate, and remove — worked at the family's pace, with the removal priced once for the whole scope. Estate executors and families settling an estate, who need a whole property cleared to a deadline they did not choose. Landlords and property managers after an eviction or a turnover, where what was left behind has to be gone before the unit can be re-let. Realtors preparing a listing. Renovators and contractors, whose trigger is a project start: the old kitchen, bathroom, flooring, or roof has to be out before the new work goes in. Businesses clearing offices, retail fixtures, and warehouse corners. Households with a single oversized problem — a hot tub, a dead refrigerator, a garage that stopped fitting a car years ago. Seasonal triggers: spring cleaning, storm debris, and the end of a lease. What every persona is buying is the same thing: the lifting, the truck, the sorting, and the lawful disposal, at one price known before the work starts.

@graph.name: Protection, Safety & Compliance
@graph.description: Protection, safety and compliance for junk removal. The handling standard is the company's moving standard: floors, walls, and doorways on the carry path are protected; pieces are carried, never dragged; standard furniture is taken apart when a piece has to come apart to leave safely, and the cleared space is walked through with the customer at the end. Pickup conditions, stated before the job: equipment that contains fuel is emptied before the appointment; a hot tub is drained and disconnected from power and water before the appointment; items for removal are the items in the surveyed scope. The regulatory boundary, stated plainly: hazardous and regulated waste is not hauled — no wet paint or solvents, no fuels, motor oil, or antifreeze, no pesticides or household chemicals, no pressurized tanks, no asbestos-containing material, no lead paint material, no medical or biohazard waste; those belong to licensed handlers and household hazardous waste routes. Refrigerant: under EPA Section 608 of the Clean Air Act (40 CFR Part 82, Subpart F), refrigerant may not be vented, and must be recovered by Section 608-certified technicians before a refrigerant-bearing appliance is processed — appliances are routed so that recovery happens; no refrigerant-recovery certification is claimed for this company. Asbestos-containing material is never disturbed — abatement is a licensed trade of its own. Dense loads are planned by weight before dispatch. Heavy assets are routed out of this service, not forced through it: gun safes and other high-mass assets of 1,500 to 3,500 lbs move under SIR Structural Integrity Relocation with L/360 floor-deflection analysis; pianos move under the piano, antique and white-glove service. Donation honesty: usable goods are routed toward donation as part of every load's sort; no donation rate or diversion percentage is claimed, and no charity is named as a partner.
